questions.q: What purpose does the editorial say calamities serve for us?
options: They show that effort is useless
Not quite. The article says: They wake us from forgetfulness and make us review how we live and what we believe.
They prove that life is governed by chance
Not quite. The article says: They wake us from forgetfulness and make us review how we live and what we believe.
They are meant only for people of the past
Not quite. The article says: They wake us from forgetfulness and make us review how we live and what we believe.
They wake us from forgetfulness and make us review how we live and what we believe
Yes. “So that perhaps they may return.”
questions.rationale: “The calamities serve the signal purpose of waking us up from our slumber of forgetfulness.”

questions.q: A police officer watching a large gathering saw a man pick up a watch someone had left behind. What did the man do with it?
options: He put it in his pocket and left
Not quite. The article says: He took it straight to the lost-property tent and then went to say his prayers.
He handed it to the officer
Not quite. The article says: He took it straight to the lost-property tent and then went to say his prayers.
He left it where it was
Not quite. The article says: He took it straight to the lost-property tent and then went to say his prayers.
He took it straight to the lost-property tent and then went to say his prayers
Right. He saw to it that it reached its owner.
questions.rationale: “The man handed over the watch without a moment’s hesitation, then he went away to say his prayers.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, does “good character conquer all”?
options: Good conduct is always rewarded with money
Not quite. The article says: Every human being is born with a moral sense, so no one can witness a truly moral act without being moved.
Every human being is born with a moral sense, so no one can witness a truly moral act without being moved
Well reasoned. Conduct persuades where speeches may not.
Rules compel people to admire it
Not quite. The article says: Every human being is born with a moral sense, so no one can witness a truly moral act without being moved.
People fear those who behave well
Not quite. The article says: Every human being is born with a moral sense, so no one can witness a truly moral act without being moved.
questions.rationale: “Human beings are endowed with moral sense as a matter of birthright. Consequently, no man can witness a truly moral act without being deeply influenced by it.”

questions.q: Where does the article say the discovery of God takes place, and where is it felt?
options: It takes place in dreams and is forgotten on waking
Not quite. The article says: It takes place in the mind, but its effect is felt through one’s entire being.
It takes place in the body and is felt in the mind
Not quite. The article says: It takes place in the mind, but its effect is felt through one’s entire being.
It takes place in the mind, but its effect is felt through one’s entire being
Yes. “As if a new sun had climbed into the sky.”
It takes place in society and is felt at home
Not quite. The article says: It takes place in the mind, but its effect is felt through one’s entire being.
questions.rationale: “The discovery of God takes place in the human mind, but a man feels its effect throughout his entire being.”

questions.q: A Companion advised his grandson: “One who does not bear with small harm from a foolish person will have to bear with great harm.” Why is this so?
options: Small harms are always imaginary
Not quite. The article says: Reacting to the first hurt sets off a chain reaction in which things go from bad to worse.
Reacting to the first hurt sets off a chain reaction in which things go from bad to worse
Right. Better to leave the sleeping ego asleep.
Foolish people are always powerful
Not quite. The article says: Reacting to the first hurt sets off a chain reaction in which things go from bad to worse.
Patience is a sign of weakness
Not quite. The article says: Reacting to the first hurt sets off a chain reaction in which things go from bad to worse.
questions.rationale: “The best way of avoiding great harm from mischief-makers is to put up with initial hurt, for, if one does not, one will set off a chain reaction in which things will go from bad to worse.”

questions.q: After its devastating defeat, what did Japan do that the article holds up as the “correct starting point”?
options: It accepted the blame for its own ruin and turned its energies to peaceful reconstruction, without complaint or nostalgia
Well read. It wasted no time bewailing lost opportunities.
It prepared quietly for another war
Not quite. The article says: It accepted the blame for its own ruin and turned its energies to peaceful reconstruction, without complaint or nostalgia.
It closed itself off from the world
Not quite. The article says: It accepted the blame for its own ruin and turned its energies to peaceful reconstruction, without complaint or nostalgia.
It waited for other nations to rebuild it
Not quite. The article says: It accepted the blame for its own ruin and turned its energies to peaceful reconstruction, without complaint or nostalgia.
questions.rationale: “Japan accepted the blame for its own destruction, and, once having done so, was able earnestly to launch itself on its own economic uplift.”

questions.q: Which image does the article use for avoiding confrontation in a world of competition?
options: A runner who pushes others aside
Not quite. The article says: A ship that veers off course for a while to avoid the reefs and so sails safely into harbour.
A climber who cuts the rope
Not quite. The article says: A ship that veers off course for a while to avoid the reefs and so sails safely into harbour.
A ship that veers off course for a while to avoid the reefs and so sails safely into harbour
Exactly. The one that sails straight at the rock is lost.
A river that breaks through a dam
Not quite. The article says: A ship that veers off course for a while to avoid the reefs and so sails safely into harbour.
questions.rationale: “It is the ship which veers temporarily off its course to avoid the reefs which will eventually sail safely into harbour.”

questions.q: Fatima, worn by housework, wished to ask her father the Prophet for a servant. What did he give her instead?
options: A share of the household of a neighbour
Not quite. The article says: Words of remembrance to say at bedtime – glorifying, praising and exalting God a hundred times in all.
A promise of help the next year
Not quite. The article says: Words of remembrance to say at bedtime – glorifying, praising and exalting God a hundred times in all.
Permission to leave the work undone
Not quite. The article says: Words of remembrance to say at bedtime – glorifying, praising and exalting God a hundred times in all.
Words of remembrance to say at bedtime – glorifying, praising and exalting God a hundred times in all
Correct. “That will do more good than a servant will.”
questions.rationale: “When you go to bed at night, glorify God 33 times, praise Him the same number of times and exalt him 34 times… That will do more good than a servant will.”

questions.q: The article begins with bacteria – tiny, yet more dangerous than the tiger. To what in our conduct does it compare them?
options: Great and obvious crimes
Not quite. The article says: Small, short-lived moments of neglect, which do the greatest damage of all.
Loud quarrels between friends
Not quite. The article says: Small, short-lived moments of neglect, which do the greatest damage of all.
Small, short-lived moments of neglect, which do the greatest damage of all
Yes. Left unchecked they become an ingrained attitude.
Honest mistakes made once
Not quite. The article says: Small, short-lived moments of neglect, which do the greatest damage of all.
questions.rationale: “The greatest damage of all is done by those seemingly insignificant and often short-lived moments of neglect… Easy-going negligence can creep into our souls, like bacteria into the body.”

questions.q: “One who does not show gratitude for lesser things will not express gratitude for greater things.” How does the article explain this?
options: Great blessings are too rare to notice
Not quite. The article says: Being thankful for a small thing opens the mind’s “file” of gratitude, bringing all its other blessings to the fore.
Being thankful for a small thing opens the mind’s “file” of gratitude, bringing all its other blessings to the fore
Well reasoned. A small thanks becomes a fountain.
Gratitude is owed only for small things
Not quite. The article says: Being thankful for a small thing opens the mind’s “file” of gratitude, bringing all its other blessings to the fore.
Small gifts are worth more than large ones
Not quite. The article says: Being thankful for a small thing opens the mind’s “file” of gratitude, bringing all its other blessings to the fore.
questions.rationale: “The file of the brain will open all the items of gratitude under this system of nature… Thus, a small event of gratitude becomes a cause of greater gratitude.”
